questions.prompt: A single-step reaction-energy profile places reactants at 20 kJ/mol, the transition-state peak at 95 kJ/mol, and products at −10 kJ/mol on one common energy scale. Which set gives forward activation energy, reverse activation energy, and overall forward energy change, respectively?
questions.explanation: A is correct. Forward activation energy is 95 − 20 = 75 kJ/mol; reverse activation energy is 95 − (−10) = 105 kJ/mol; the forward endpoint change is −10 − 20 = −30 kJ/mol. B treats absolute plotted levels as the required energy differences. C mishandles the negative product level and reverses the endpoint-change sign. D exchanges the forward and reverse starting levels. Activation energy is measured from the relevant reactants, not from an arbitrary zero.

questions.prompt: An elementary profile has reactant energy −20 kJ/mol, product energy +10 kJ/mol, and peak energy +30 kJ/mol. Which description is consistent with this profile?
options: Energy-releasing forward change, with forward barrier 10 kJ/mol.
Energy-absorbing forward change, with forward barrier 30 kJ/mol.
Energy-releasing forward change, with reverse barrier 50 kJ/mol.
Energy-absorbing forward change of 30 kJ/mol, with forward barrier 50 kJ/mol.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Products lie 10 − (−20) = 30 kJ/mol above reactants, while the peak is 30 − (−20) = 50 kJ/mol above reactants. A and C reverse the endpoint energy direction. B gives the absolute peak value rather than the gap from reactants. The reverse barrier is 30 − 10 = 20 kJ/mol, not the forward barrier. The profile depicts energy, so these conclusions do not require a separate entropy or equilibrium calculation.

questions.prompt: Two hypothetical elementary pathways share reactant level 0 kJ/mol and product level −25 kJ/mol. Path I has peak 40 kJ/mol; path II has peak 70 kJ/mol. At the same temperature, assume equal encounter and orientation factors. What comparison is supported?
options: II must be faster because a higher peak releases more endpoint energy.
I is expected to be faster because its lower forward barrier can be crossed by a larger energetic fraction, while the endpoint energy change is the same.
The rates must be equal because the product energies are equal.
I must form a different product because its peak energy differs.
questions.explanation: B is correct. With other kinetic factors explicitly matched, I has a smaller activation-energy requirement, so more encounters can cross it. Both pathways have endpoint change −25 kJ/mol. A confuses peak height with net released energy. C treats equal endpoint energy as equal kinetic barrier. D contradicts the supplied shared endpoints. An energy profile alone would not fix every real pathway's encounter/orientation factors; those are controlled here.

questions.prompt: A graphing program adds 200 kJ/mol to every vertical energy value in a reaction profile, changing only the chosen zero of energy. How do forward activation energy and overall energy change respond?
options: Both increase by 200 kJ/mol.
Activation energy increases, but overall change stays the same.
Both remain unchanged because each is a difference between two levels shifted by the same amount.
Both become zero because the energy reference was changed.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Subtracting shifted levels cancels the common offset: (E_peak + 200) − (E_reactants + 200) equals the original barrier, and the endpoint difference behaves the same way. A and B treat a reference shift as a physical change in a gap. D incorrectly erases relative energies. Only vertical differences, not the absolute zero chosen for plotting, determine these quantities.

questions.prompt: What does the horizontal reaction-coordinate axis of an elementary energy profile represent?
options: A collective description of the structural motions and rearrangements connecting reactants to products, rather than an elapsed-time scale.
Elapsed time, so the horizontal width of a peak directly gives reaction duration.
The number of molecules that must be present in the laboratory vessel.
Temperature, so moving right always means the sample becomes hotter.
questions.explanation: A is correct. Reaction coordinate tracks progress through molecular rearrangement along the represented pathway. B mistakes it for a kinetic time trace; width alone does not measure reaction duration. C substitutes particle inventory for structural progress. D substitutes temperature for reaction coordinate. The vertical axis gives energy along that coordinate, not how much time a sample spends at each position.

questions.prompt: For an unchanged elementary pathway, heating increases the measured rate. Which explanation is compatible with keeping the same reactant, product, and transition-state levels on a simplified energy profile?
options: The activation energy must fall because any faster rate requires a lower drawn peak.
The distribution changes so that a larger fraction of encounters can reach the same transition-state energy requirement.
The products must move below the reactants even if the original change was energy-absorbing.
Heating removes the need for reactants to pass through any transition-state region.
questions.explanation: B is correct. Rate can increase because the energetic population changes without changing the pathway's simplified barrier. A equates every rate increase with a barrier decrease. C invents a change in endpoint energy ordering. D removes the pathway requirement instead of explaining increased access to it. This is a qualitative temperature argument, not an Arrhenius-equation calculation or a claim that all thermodynamic levels are exactly temperature-independent in every detailed model.

questions.prompt: For one single-peak pathway, define ΔE = E_products − E_reactants, E_a,f = E_peak − E_reactants, and E_a,r = E_peak − E_products. Which relationship follows?
options: ΔE = E_a,f + E_a,r
ΔE = E_a,r − E_a,f
ΔE = E_a,f × E_a,r
ΔE = E_a,f − E_a,r
questions.explanation: D is correct. Subtracting the reverse barrier from the forward barrier cancels E_peak and leaves E_products − E_reactants. A adds the barriers instead of eliminating their shared peak. B reverses the endpoint-change sign. C has squared-energy units and cannot represent an energy difference. For energy-releasing forward reactions, the forward barrier is smaller than the reverse barrier along this same pathway.

questions.prompt: A reaction profile has reactants at 0 kJ/mol, products at −40 kJ/mol, and a peak at +50 kJ/mol. Why does the product level alone not establish that the reaction will occur rapidly at room temperature?
options: A negative endpoint change means the forward activation energy must also be negative.
Energy-releasing reactions cannot have transition states.
The forward process still has a 50 kJ/mol barrier; favorable endpoint energy does not by itself specify how many encounters can cross it per time.
A lower-energy product can form only after all particles have exactly the peak energy.
questions.explanation: C is correct. The endpoint difference describes net energy change, whereas rate depends on access to the barrier and other kinetic factors. A confuses ΔE with activation energy. B incorrectly removes barriers from energy-releasing processes. D replaces an energy distribution with a single shared value for all particles. The profile supports a positive forward barrier, not an unconditional room-temperature speed prediction.

questions.prompt: In a one-step energy profile, what is the most appropriate interpretation of the molecular arrangement at its single maximum?
options: A final stable product that accumulates because it has the highest energy.
A measure of the average temperature of all molecules in the sample.
The reactant mixture before any structural rearrangement has begun.
A transition-state arrangement along the pathway, associated with the barrier between reactants and products.
questions.explanation: D is correct. The maximum corresponds to the transition-state region of the specified elementary pathway. A mistakes a barrier maximum for a stable product level. B confuses pathway potential energy with a bulk temperature measurement. C places the unmodified starting state at the peak despite the profile's separate reactant level. The diagram is a representation along a coordinate, not a claim that this maximum is an isolatable accumulated substance.

questions.prompt: An elementary forward reaction has activation energy 30 kJ/mol and overall energy change ΔE = −70 kJ/mol. Along the same pathway, what is the reverse activation energy?
options: 40 kJ/mol
100 kJ/mol
−40 kJ/mol
70 kJ/mol
questions.explanation: B is correct. E_a,r = E_a,f − ΔE = 30 − (−70) = 100 kJ/mol. With reactants chosen as zero, the peak is +30 and products −70, giving the same 100 kJ/mol gap. A subtracts the magnitudes without retaining the sign. C adds the signed endpoint change to the forward barrier and gives a negative reverse barrier inconsistent with this single-peak model. D confuses the magnitude of net energy change with the full reverse climb.

questions.prompt: A proposed simple single-peak profile places reactants at 0, the claimed highest transition-state peak at +30, and products at +40 kJ/mol. The drawing is meant to rise from reactants through that sole maximum and then descend to products. Which evaluation is correct?
options: It is automatically valid because every activation energy can be smaller than any product level without qualification.
It becomes valid merely by increasing temperature, without changing any plotted level or the claimed shape.
The levels are inconsistent with the stated sole-maximum-then-descent shape because the products lie above the claimed highest peak.
It is invalid only because energy-absorbing reactions can never occur.
questions.explanation: C is correct. A curve descending from its highest +30 level cannot end at +40; the supplied simple peak description and numerical levels cannot all hold. A overlooks that internal graphical inconsistency. B changes the particle-energy population but does not repair the stated ordering of plotted levels. D wrongly excludes energy-absorbing reactions rather than addressing this drawing. This check concerns the explicitly claimed simple profile, not every possible barrierless or more complex pathway.
